subject: Communication
title: The Framing Effect
description: A 60-second lesson on The Framing Effect.

hook.text: '90% fat-free' and '10% fat' are the same thing. But one sells yogurt. The other kills sales.

buildup.text: The framing effect means how information is presented changes decisions — even when the facts are identical.

discovery.text: Tversky and Kahneman showed that people choose differently when outcomes are framed as gains versus losses.

twist.text: Doctors describing surgery as '90% survival rate' get more consent than '10% mortality rate.' Same stat.

climax.text: Politicians, marketers, and negotiators choose frames carefully. Whoever sets the frame controls the choice.

punchline.text: Facts don't change. Frames change everything.

quiz.question: What does the framing effect demonstrate?
options: Presentation changes decisions even with identical facts

details.summary: How information is presented changes decisions even when the underlying facts are identical. Saying 90 percent survival rate feels different from 10 percent mortality rate. Framing exploits the way our brains process gains versus losses differently.
details.whyItMatters: Politicians, journalists, and marketers frame every message. Recognizing framing lets you evaluate content based on substance rather than presentation.
takeaways: Identical facts framed differently lead to different decisions
Loss frames are more emotionally powerful than gain frames
Reframing is a core skill in negotiation and leadership

faq.question: What is the classic framing effect experiment?
faq.answer: Tversky and Kahneman's Asian disease problem presented identical survival statistics in gain versus loss frames. When framed as lives saved, people chose the safe option. When framed as lives lost, people chose the risky gamble. The facts were identical both times.

faq.question: How can you detect framing in news media?
faq.answer: Look for emotionally charged language, selective statistics, and one-sided presentation of facts. Restate claims in neutral terms and consider the opposite frame. If the headline says costs taxpayers millions, ask what the same money produces in benefits.
